Valérie Plagnol

13 October 2026

Valérie Plagnol

Economist, member of the Foundation’s scientific committee

### “Out of Debt…”

In the wake of the subprime crisis, the markets grouped under the acronym ‘PIIGs’ the so-called ‘ Club Med’ countries of Southern Europe together with Ireland. Having managed to avoid the property crisis and still enjoying some room for manoeuvre, France managed to look on at a distance and, although it was hit hard by the euro crisis in the years that followed, its credit rating remained strong and its credibility intact.

According to Eurostat, Ireland has definitively left the PIIGs, with gross debt falling to 37% of its GDP in the first quarter of 2026. Portugal has reduced its debt to 91% of GDP. France, on the other hand, has joined the club of ‘100 % and above’ countries (117.6%). Belgium (109.1%) and Italy (138.9%) have been long-standing members. Spain joined this group in the wake of its property bubble bursting and is struggling to fall back below the 100 % threshold (101.6%). Greece’s public debt still stands at 143.5% of its GDP, illustrating just how painful it is to stabilise and furthermore reduce its debt. However, as the chart below shows, the debt-reduction efforts undertaken in Greece, Portugal and even Italy stand in stark contrast to France’s persisting deterioration.

## “Risky France”

From the perspective of international markets, France has indeed become a problem for Europe. And is there a risk that this could spread? Indeed, the yield on the 10-year OAT is approaching 5% (4.89%), representing a spread of more than 130 basis points (bp) over the German Bund – a level not seen since the euro crisis. Not only is French debt trading at higher yields than that of Italy or Greece, but against a backdrop of widespread pressure on global interest rates, it could end up dragging other countries down with it and undermining the efforts currently underway.

## Creditor’s confidence

Admittedly a state is not a household: it does not die, it levies taxes, and its debt is rolled over far more often than it is repaid. Consequently, many people have for too long claimed that states could not be subject to budgetary discipline. However, this leeway comes at a price: it is valid only for as long as its creditors place their trust in it.

And it would appear that in France, we have reached a point where this issue has become sufficiently pressing to demand that we tackle it with courage and determination. Is there any need to emphasise the urgency of the situation? On the eve of the budget’s presentation to Parliament, Agence France Trésor announced that it will need to raise nearly €340 billion (339.7) on the markets next year, based on a deficit of 5% of GDP as set out in the draft Finance Bill for 2027. The bulk of the additional €28 billion (19.4) to be raised compared with last year is due to higher amortisation: securities issued during the years of ultra-low interest rates are gradually maturing and must be refinanced on far less favourable terms. The average yield on medium- and long-term emissions rose from 3.14 % in 2025 to 3.55 % in 2026. The government’s debt service costs are therefore expected to surge from €62.6 billion to €72.9 billion in 2027: an additional €10 billion in a single year, which is more than the projected increase in the defence budget.

With debt estimated at 119.3% of GDP by the end of 2026, rising to 121.7% by the end of 2027, France is returning to levels not seen since the immediate post-war period. It was not alone in this situation at the time, but the circumstances were very different. Subject to rationing until 1949 and rampant inflation, and with the support of substantial aid from the Marshall Plan between 1948 and 1952, France was able to begin its reconstruction and reduce its debt, despite the cost of the colonial wars. Moreover, there was severe ‘ financial repression’[1]. In other words, it was primarily inflation and captive savings that ‘paid off’ the post-war debt.

## Five solutions, nothing more, nothing less

As many experts have reminded us, there are not many ways to stabilise and then reduce public debt. Following the subprime crisis in 2013, Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff sounded the alarm, noting that the current level of public debt in advanced economies is approaching the highest levels seen in two centuries. Let’s take a look at them, from the most encouraging to the most painful.

### 1. Economic Growth

It all comes down to the gap between the apparent interest rate on the debt and the rate of nominal growth[2]. The apparent rate represents the sum of interest paid divided by the total outstanding debt. It is estimated at 2.1% in 2026, above the nominal growth expected this year, increasing by 1.4 % and 1.7% respectively, based on volume growth of 0.4% When the apparent rate exceeds growth, the debt feeds on itself: this is the famous ‘ snowball effect’. However, as refinancing takes place, this apparent rate can only converge towards market rates, with the 10-year OAT now trading above 4.9%. Growth remains the least painful solution, but it cannot be imposed: it requires investment, productivity gains and reforms, the benefits of which can only be reaped in the medium term.

### 2. Fiscal adjustment

Reducing debt begins when we stop contributing to it. To achieve this, public administrations must ensure that at least their primary balance – that is, excluding interest payments – is in balance, and even in surplus once the apparent rate exceeds growth. With a deficit of 5% of GDP and interest payments of over €72 billion, our primary deficit will still be around 2.5% of GDP; the effort still required therefore far exceeds the €54 billion in savings announced for 2027. Others have achieved this: Canada and Sweden in the 1990s, and more recently Portugal, Cyprus and Greece, whose debt-to-GDP ratios fell by between 20 and 30% of the GDP between 2022 and 2025. Experience shows that these adjustments are even more successful when they focus on expenditure, are implemented over the long term and are accompanied by growth-friendly reforms.

### 3. Financial repression, accompanied by a steady dose of inflation

This involves channelling domestic savings – voluntarily or under regulatory constraint – towards government financing at rates below the rate of inflation: bonds issued directly to the public, caps on interest payments, prudential rules requiring banks and insurers to hold public debt, targeted tax incentives, and even restrictions on capital outflows. According to Carmen Reinhart and Belén Sbrancia, this mechanism helped the United States and the United Kingdom to ‘write off’ the equivalent of 3 to 4% of GDP in debt per year during the post-war decades. In the eurozone, where monetary policy is the responsibility of the ECB and capital flows freely, its more drastic forms are ruled out. Its milder forms, however, remain possible: any ‘channelling’ of savings deserves to be examined in this light. Through euro-denominated life insurance funds, French savers are already among the government’s leading creditors. They would therefore also be the first to be exposed to returns that are consistently below inflation.

### 4. An inflationary surprise, that is to say, an unexpected surge in inflation

The price spike of 2022–2023 provided a recent illustration of this: by inflating nominal GDP, it caused France’s debt-to-GDP ratio to fall by nearly 2% in a year. However, this is a one-off, achieved at the expense of savers holding fixed-rate assets, and the markets subsequently make them pay for it through a higher risk premium. 

### 5. Explicit default or debt restructuring

This is a last resort. Greece tried it in 2012, forcing its private creditors to accept a write-down of more than half the face value of their bonds, at the cost of deep recession and prolonged exclusion from the markets.

## A reputation shaped by history

Let us take a long-term view. France has not formally defaulted on its domestic debt since 1797 and the ‘two-thirds bankruptcy’ – a measure to restore public finances carried out by the Directory at the end of the Reign of Terror and before the Consulate. Building on this experience, Louis XVIII, upon his return to the throne, had Article 70 of the Charter of 1814 stipulate that: “ The public debt is guaranteed. Any commitment entered into by the State with its creditors is inviolable.” This commitment laid the foundations for the reputation of France’s creditworthiness. It reaped the benefits of this in 1871–1872: the loans issued by Adolphe Thiers to pay the indemnity of 5 billion francs demanded by Prussia were massively oversubscribed, and the debt was settled before it fell due.

This creditworthiness was put to the test in the aftermath of the First World War. The interwar period illustrates the reduction of domestic debt through inflation and devaluation: the 1928 Poincaré franc was worth no more than one-fifth of the Germinal franc, cementing what Keynes called ‘ the euthanasia of the rentier’. As for the external debt owed to the Allies, it was partly written off. France was counting on German reparations to meet these obligations. But Weimar Germany, ruined by the hyperinflation of 1923, was unable to honour its commitments, and France in turn suspended its repayments to the United States at the end of 1932.

A distinction must therefore be drawn between domestic and external debt. The latter, denominated in foreign currency – often a hard currency – requires the debtor to increase their exports at the expense of domestic consumption in order to accumulate foreign exchange reserves. Inflation and devaluation therefore only serve to undermine its ability to meet these obligations. The debt crises in emerging economies during the 1980s and 1990s – from Latin America to Asia and Russia – amply demonstrated this, necessitating severe austerity measures comprising tax hikes, financial crackdowns and restructuring.

The so-called advanced economies are therefore not about to give up this hard-won credibility, which allows them to borrow in their own currency. France, like the 21 members of the euro area, thus occupies a unique position: it borrows in euro, a currency it shares but does not issue on its own. The sovereign debt crisis of 2010–2012 served as a reminder that a eurozone member state can find itself at the mercy of market sentiment. It incurs debt in a currency it does not issue, and the treaties rule out any solidarity regarding national debts: Article 125 of the TFEU proscribes both the Union and other Member States from assuming the liabilities of a Member State (the ‘ no bail-out’ clause), and Article 123 prohibits the ECB from directly financing Member States. This principle is a corollary of the Member States’ fiscal sovereignty. It was coupled with convergence criteria relating to deficits, debt, inflation and interest rates. Far from being arbitrary, these criteria sought to prevent the emergence of centrifugal forces in an area where capital circulates freely.

The crisis forced further action to supplement this framework. In 2012, the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) was established to lend to Member States in difficulty, in exchange for an adjustment programme. In the same year, Mario Draghi’s ‘ whatever it takes’ was followed by the announcement of Outright Monetary Transactions (OMTs). This programme was never activated, but it was enough on its own to stem speculation against Italian debt. It remains, however, conditional upon an ESM programme.

Later, massive purchases of government bonds effectively acted as a buffer: the Public Sector Purchase Programme (PSPP) from 2015, followed by the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP) in 2020, with flexibility in the allocation of funds across countries.
